verdict.note: The review completed and grounds all three planted defects in specific source lines: tenant binding (design.md:9,23-24 vs :18-19), the false KeyError claim (design.md:26 vs src/flags.py:12), and 6×200=1,200/s below 1,800/s (design.md:13,54-57); its added finding that schema creation happens only in staging (design.md:60 vs :62-64) matches the literal rollout text, and its uncertainties explicitly treat H1 and H2 as consistent with the accepted ADRs.

The review correctly identifies both critical defects and the capacity shortfall, cites sources for each, adds two grounded extra findings (report rows defaulting to bucket 'incoming', and the rollout backlog deleting not-yet-uploaded pending rows plus duplicating jobs), and makes no claim that contradicts H1 or H2.

The review correctly detects all three planted defects with accurate source evidence (the tenant-less cache key read before authorization, the 120-per-10-second ceiling of 720 per minute against the required 900, and invoke returning Outcome(ok=False) instead of raising), adds one grounded low-severity finding (a cache-fill race against terminal eviction, plus retry transitions that do not evict, per design.md:55,61-64), and affirms rather than violates both hard negatives.

The review completed and cites concrete source lines; it reports no findings, which is correct for a case with no planted defect, and its four uncertainties are conditional and recorded separately, not counted as false alarms or hard-negative violations. The first uncertainty questions the R3 bound only conditionally and does not contradict H2.

The review correctly found all three planted defects with accurate source citations: v1 decimal strings vs ADR-001 integer cents, discount_cents never checking expires_at, and aggregate tax rounding vs G4 per-line rounding (the 2×5-cent example checks out at 2 vs 1 cent). It made no false claims and did not contradict shipping tax exemption or minimum-spend eligibility.

unsupported_claims.claim: The 550-per-shard requirement conflicts with ADR-003's 560 admission limit and the 2,240 rollout capacity.
unsupported_claims.why: docs/design.md:9 describes the load to support: 2,200 requests/s with at most 550 arriving per shard. It is not a cap on admission. ADR-003 admits 560 per shard (2,240 total, docs/adr-003-refresh-capacity.md:9-11), which covers 550 per shard and 2,200 total. docs/design.md:69 is consistent with that, so the sources contain no conflict.

unsupported_claims.claim: The implementation plan is deficient because it does not name the files to change.
unsupported_claims.why: No source requires a file-level plan. The finding imposes a preferred template rather than identifying a defect. docs/design.md:62-75 gives a concrete migration, gating, legacy-handler, client-persistence, canary, test and rollback plan.

verdict.note: The review completed but has no valid findings: the capacity finding misreads the 550-per-shard load as a cap and contradicts H4, and the file-list finding imposes a template rather than citing a defect.

The review is complete and grounded, and it detects all three planted defects. Finding 3 is the stale-value backfill race (C1), finding 1 is the same-deploy contract that violates ADR-002 and R4 (C2), and finding 2 is the ~66.7 h backfill against R2's 6 h target (M1); the first uncertainty doubts the R1 lock bound, but it is recorded as an uncertainty rather than a finding, so H2 is not violated.

unsupported_claims.claim: No component reads usage_adjustments or sets billed_in, so late events (>48 h) are counted nowhere in billing, violating R1 (finding 4).
unsupported_claims.why: ADR-001:12-14 is an accepted decision stating the billing service reads unbilled usage_adjustments directly when building the next invoice and sets billed_in. The design's exporter reading only closed rollups does not remove that path, and the review itself cites these ADR lines, so late usage is billed one cycle later rather than lost.

unsupported_claims.claim: The archive lacks ADR-002's tenant/date partitioning, so per-tenant disputes require scanning every tenant's files (finding 5, first half).
unsupported_claims.why: ADR-002:10-11 is accepted and explicitly specifies hourly Parquet partitioned by tenant and date. The design's brief archiver section does not contradict or supersede it, so asserting the partitioning is absent is not supported.

verdict.note: The review correctly detects all three planted defects (C2, C1 and M1) with precise source evidence, counts one grounded extra point (the archive retains duplicate event_ids, so rebuilds need dedup), but violates H1 by claiming adjustments are never billed despite ADR-001.

unsupported_claims.claim: Finding 4 says the self_service_export flag is only described as gating API/button routing, not the worker.
unsupported_claims.why: design.md:86-87 says the API and the worker ship behind the flag, and design.md:96-97 says queued rows are processed once the flag is back on. The worker is therefore stated to be gated. The finding's main rollback point, that after step 4 there is no fulfilment path while the flag is off, is still grounded.

verdict.note: The review completed and found all three planted defects: C1 (cross-account export to a caller-chosen email), M1 (960 vs 1,200/day), and C2 (dropping export_tasks with ~300 open deadlines, plus the rollback gap). Three additional findings are grounded: the rollback leaves no export path after step 4, the 6-minute benchmark omits support tickets, gzip, upload and email, and the staff-account comparison cannot validate support_tickets. One sub-claim about the flag's scope contradicts design.md:86. Finding 7 (implementation details left open) is a template-style completeness observation and is not counted either way. No hard negatives are violated: the review keeps ADR-001 and ADR-002 as accepted decisions.

The review completed with three grounded findings: aggregate tax rounding (C1, with a correct 5+5 cent counterexample), expired coupons accepted because discount_cents never checks expires_at (M1), and v1 decimal strings contradicting ADR-001 (M2); it makes no false claims and does not contradict H1 or H2, and its eight uncertainties are questions or conditional risks.

The review correctly identifies the locale/date HTML cache privacy leak (C1), the 120,000-versus-180,000 dispatch capacity shortfall (M1), and the LIMIT 100 truncation contradicting the 'complete pending set' claim (M2), with no false alarms or hard-negative violations.

The review found all three planted defects with accurate source citations. Its per-line rounding counterexample is correct (two 5-cent lines at 10% give 1+1=2 cents versus 1 cent), and it made no claims that contradict H1 or H2.

The review completed with source-grounded findings that correctly detect C1 (unscoped SELECT at design.md:66 vs. tenant-filtered get_delivery), M1 (24 slots × 30/min = 720 < 1,200), and M2 (result['id'] vs. fetchone()[0] scalar return); it adds one grounded finding that the 14-day retention requirement (design.md:14) has no timestamp column or cleanup step in the schema or rollout, and it correctly treats sandbox HTTP and unordered dispatch as permitted by ADR-002 and ADR-001.

The review grounds all three planted defects in the sources: missing DELETE publication versus R5/ADR-002, non-idempotent balance deltas under at-least-once delivery, and the 37,500 s rebuild exceeding the 8-hour window. It makes no extra concrete claims and does not contradict either hard negative.

The review grounds all three planted defects in specific source lines: per-line versus aggregate tax rounding (with a correct 22-versus-21-cent counterexample), the false claim that discount_cents checks expiry, and v1 decimal strings contradicting ADR-001; it also adds one defensible minor finding that design.md:22 misdescribes tax_cents, and it violates no hard negatives.

The review completed with three source-grounded findings that correctly match C1 (cache hit bypasses tenant check), M2 (invoke returns Outcome(ok=False) rather than raising, so failures become successes), and M1 (720/min dispatcher ceiling below 900/min); it makes no unsupported claims or hard-negative violations, and its two uncertainties are recorded separately.

unsupported_claims.claim: Sandbox dispatch does not follow accepted ADR-002: plain-HTTP sandbox requests go directly from production workers to arbitrary destinations, and nothing keeps the sandbox and production queues apart.
unsupported_claims.why: design.md:16 explicitly says sandbox follows ADR-002, and design.md:51 defers HTTP use to that environment policy. ADR-002:7 accepts HTTP sandbox registrations as an isolated-environment exception, and ADR-002:11 has the dispatcher use the endpoint's registered environment, which endpoints.environment records (design.md:56). The missing environment column on deliveries is irrelevant because each delivery is tied to its endpoint through endpoint_id. The finding treats the accepted sandbox HTTP arrangement as a defect.

verdict.note: The review detects all three planted defects (C1 cross-tenant leak, M1 720/min capacity ceiling, M2 int-indexed-as-mapping) and adds three grounded gaps (unspecified next_at/attempt_count on insert, no tenant gating for staged rollout, no retention step), but its sandbox finding contradicts the accepted ADR-002 exception (H1).

The review completed with grounded, source-cited findings. It correctly identifies the refund-model mismatch (C1), the detail-endpoint IDOR (C2, rated high rather than critical) and the undefined HoldPolicy (M1). It adds five grounded findings: the manual-to-automated cutover double-pay boundary, unspecified webhook signature verification and mapping, the unsourced destination account data, the missing carried-balance view required by ADR-001, and the absence of webhook/API build phases in the rollout. It keeps the correct $25 carry-forward and throughput arithmetic out of its defect list.

The review completed with no concrete findings, which is correct for this no-defect case; its three uncertainties are grounded questions about pending benchmarks, unimplemented atomicity, and the manual-import checked_at source, and none contradicts H1–H4.

unsupported_claims.claim: Sandbox dispatch does not use the gateway required by ADR-002, so workers send sandbox HTTP traffic directly to registered URLs.
unsupported_claims.why: The design states that sandbox follows ADR-002 (design.md:16) and that sandbox HTTP is used 'as specified by the environment policy' (design.md:51). That incorporates the accepted gateway rule (adr-002:7,11). 'Dispatch uses the registered URL' (design.md:50) names the destination and is compatible with routing through the gateway, so the direct-send conflict is inferred, not shown. The finding does not claim that sandbox HTTP breaks the production HTTPS rule, so H1 is not listed as violated.

verdict.note: The review detects all three planted defects (C1 tenant leak, M1 720/min capacity, M2 integer-vs-mapping return). It adds two grounded findings (no per-tenant rollout mechanism; no schema or process support for 14-day retention) and one unsupported sandbox-gateway claim that ignores the design's explicit deferral to ADR-002.

The review completed with three source-grounded findings that map one-to-one to C2 (export authorization uses the body tenant_id), C1 (a queued purge is not synchronized with a later acknowledged hold), and M1 (240 GiB at 2 GiB/min takes 120 minutes against a 90-minute requirement); it has no false claims, violates no hard negatives, and records two uncertainties separately.

The review completed and correctly detected C1 (no email match on accept), C2 (retry re-runs add_member's unconditional seat increment and billing report), and M1 (10 msg/s cap makes 500 emails need ~50 s); it made no false claims and did not contradict H1 or H2, and its three uncertainties are recorded separately and not counted.

The review completed with no findings, which correctly matches a case with no planted defects; its three uncertainties are grounded in the sources (docs/design.md:7,10,13; src/lookup.py:6-14) and none of them contradicts any hard negative.

The review grounds all four planted defects in the sources. Its unfiltered-replay finding (design.md:13) is the same monotonic-state defect as C1, so it gets no separate credit, and the ten uncertainties are recorded separately without being counted as false alarms.

The review correctly detects all three planted defects. M2 includes accurate backlog arithmetic: 10 jobs/s growth, the 60 s wait exceeded at about 120 s, and about 6,000 jobs queued at 10 minutes. It adds three grounded findings: the outbox schema lacks creation and expiry data, rollback retention conflicts with expiry cleanup, and the adapter has no transient/permanent distinction. It contradicts neither hard negative.

The review completed with grounded findings; it correctly detects the X-Account-ID quota bypass (C1), the ADR-002 per-request PostgreSQL violation (M1) and the 16,000 vs 24,000 shard capacity shortfall (M2); it also makes five valid additional findings (hot-shard skew from the 10,000/s limit, rollback to the hardcoded 100/worker limiter, the undefined policy revision for the replay gate, the unplanned restart blocking, and the undefined request ID), and it neither contradicts the fixed-window nor the /healthz hard negatives.

unsupported_claims.claim: The design and rollout leave out billing of late usage from usage_adjustments, so late events for migrated tenants may never be invoiced.
unsupported_claims.why: Accepted ADR-001 (docs/adr-001-event-time-windows.md:12-14) already assigns this to the billing service, which reads unbilled adjustments directly and sets billed_in. The design's R4 and the exporter reading only closed usage_hourly rows (design.md:20, 57-58) are consistent with that decision. The design does not need to restate it, and late usage is not left unbilled (H1). The finding hedges ('If billing does not already read it'), so it is unsupported rather than a direct assertion that H1 is false.

verdict.note: The review grounds and detects all three planted defects (C2 tenant_id not overwritten, C1 1h dedup vs 24h client retries, M1 48k<60k events/s); its adjustments-billing finding is unsupported given accepted ADR-001, and its archive-detail omission is a grounded low-severity extra that correctly concedes 400 days covers 13 months.

unsupported_claims.claim: The 50-second rollback bound omits assignment-fetch latency, so R3's 60-second guarantee does not follow from the design.
unsupported_claims.why: The design's worst case (docs/design.md:44-46) is a 20 s poll plus the 30 s request deadline, which is 50 s and under 60 s. Rollback needs no model load (lines 41-42). Concluding that R3 is not met asserts the opposite of hard negative H2.

unsupported_claims.claim: The implementation plan does not name the files that implement its migration, endpoints, authorization or feature flag.
unsupported_claims.why: Nothing in the sources requires a design doc to list implementation file paths. The rollout plan (docs/design.md:84-93) gives phases with done-criteria. This is a template preference, which the protocol says not to treat as a requirement, not a defect.

verdict.note: No defect was planted; the review has two grounded extra findings (no canary load/readiness step before routing, and rollout_events has no version identifier), one finding that contradicts H2 on R3 latency, and one template-style finding about missing file paths.

All three findings are grounded and correct. The first gives the reverse example (a reset token verifying an email) but names the same root defect, that purpose is never checked against the route, so it counts as C1. The capacity math (18,000 jobs against 12,000 or 13,200 send starts) is accurate, the 60-minute versus 24-hour conflict is correctly cited, and the uncertainties are consistent with H1 and H2.

The review detects the locale-keyed private HTML cache, the LIMIT 100 truncation and the 120,000-per-hour capacity shortfall, and adds one grounded finding: operator address correction (design.md:44) conflicts with payload immutability (design.md:60) and has no defined failed-to-prepared transition; it violates neither hard negative.

The review correctly detects all three planted defects, adds one grounded finding (ingest accepts an event with a non-parseable timestamp, per src/ingest_api.py:32-37), and treats the late-adjustment billing path consistently with H1.

The review completed with three source-grounded findings that correctly match C2 (ingest forwards the payload tenant_id), M1 (16 × 3,000 = 48,000 is below the 60,000 events/s peak) and C1 (1-hour dedup retention against 24-hour client retries); its uncertainties explicitly affirm H1 and H2 rather than violating them.

All three findings are grounded and correct and map one-to-one to C1, M1 (24 slots × 30/min = 720 < 1,200) and M2; the sandbox HTTP and unordered-delivery hard negatives are treated as accepted rather than as defects.

The review completed and found all three planted defects (C1, C2, M1) with correct source evidence, and it did not violate either hard negative. Two extra findings are grounded and valid: bulk invites taking over the shared 10 msg/s mail-out capacity (adr-002:11-12), and the unspecified ordering and partial-failure handling between commit and enqueue (design.md:34-35, 83-84). The low-severity finding about missing files, tests and rollback is a template or style observation, so it counts neither as a valid finding nor as a false alarm.

The review is complete and grounded in the sources, it correctly detects all three planted defects (the X-Account-ID quota bypass, per-request PostgreSQL reads against ADR-002, and 16,000 vs 24,000 shard capacity) without violating either hard negative, and it raises four non-counted uncertainties.

The review correctly finds all three planted defects with accurate source citations: the cache hit that bypasses tenant checks, the 720-per-minute dispatcher ceiling, and the misread invoke contract; it makes no unsupported claims and keeps lease-recovery and ADR-002 concerns as conditional uncertainties without contradicting H1 or H2.

The review grounds all three planted defects in specific source lines: the expiry check missing from discount_cents, aggregate tax rounding (its 5+5 cent counterexample checks out at 2 vs 1 cent), and decimal strings conflicting with ADR-001. It contradicts no hard negatives, though it rates the critical tax-rounding defect only medium.

The review is complete and grounded: it catches the X-Account-ID quota bypass, the per-request PostgreSQL reads that violate ADR-002, and the 16,000/sec vs 24,000/sec shard shortfall; it adds two valid findings (a per-account limit of 10,000/sec exceeds one shard's 4,000/sec capacity, and logged data cannot reconstruct the replay gate) and violates neither hard negative.

The review correctly identifies all three planted defects with source-grounded evidence: the tenant_id overwrite claim contradicted by ingest_api.py:21-37, 48,000 events/s capacity against the 60,000 events/s peak, and 1-hour dedup retention against 24-hour client retries. Three grounded additional findings are counted as valid: adjustments are left out of the rollout comparison and phased billing, R3 has no serving mechanism, and client timestamps get no range check. The rollout-completeness finding is factually accurate but rests on template expectations (files, tests, rollback), so it is not counted. Neither hard negative is contradicted, since the review acknowledges that ADR-001 bills adjustments and does not dispute the 400-day retention.

The review detects all three planted defects with source-grounded evidence and violates no hard negatives; its extra finding, that step 1's expiry check returns 410 to a retry of an accept that committed near expiry, is valid because design.md:50-51 applies the check before the accepted-retry path at 57-60 with no exemption.

All three findings are grounded in the sources and map to C1, C2 and M1 (C1 and C2 are labeled major rather than critical); the review raises neither hard negative, and its seven uncertainties are open questions, not false alarms.

unsupported_claims.claim: Finding 3: the export source and row-count baseline are undefined, so the abandon condition cannot be implemented, and nothing in the design guarantees tenant scoping in queries.
unsupported_claims.why: design.md:21-22 copies 'from one consistent export' and checks row counts against that export, which is an implementable check. Tenant scoping is an accepted decision: ADR-002:10-11 requires tenant_id in every query and cache key, design.md:32 adopts it, snapshot_reader.py:25 binds tenant_id and cache.py:13 keys on it. The rest of the finding (no chart_id-to-SQL mapping, no named flag system) is a completeness/template observation, not a defect in the design's logic.

verdict.note: No planted defects; findings 1 (cron schemas created between rollout phases 1 and 2 get no snapshot_log row, so retention, cleanup and snapctl rollback skip them) and 2 (cache hits return json.dumps(default=str) values, so taken_at and numeric types differ from misses) are grounded additional findings, finding 3 is unsupported, and finding 4 is a style/completeness observation not counted either way.

The review correctly detects all three planted defects (the X-Account-ID quota evasion, per-request PostgreSQL reads contrary to ADR-002, and the 16,000 vs 24,000 capacity shortfall), adds two grounded findings (an unevaluable replay gate with a weaker resume condition, and the counting-flow versus exactly-once contradiction), treats the Markdown list-continuation finding as a style observation alongside 11 uncertainties, and makes no claim against the fixed-window or /healthz hard negatives.

The review completed with three grounded findings: the hold-vs-queued-purge race (C1), cross-tenant export through the request-body tenant_id (C2), and the 120-minute lower bound against the 90-minute deadline (M1); its five uncertainties are not counted as false alarms, and it explicitly affirms the canonical-archive and tenant-scoped identity decisions rather than contradicting H1 or H2.

The review's three grounded findings map to C1 (X-Account-ID quota evasion), M1 (per-request PostgreSQL reads violating ADR-002), and M2 (16,000 vs 24,000 capacity shortfall), and it makes no false claims against H1 or H2 (its restart uncertainty explicitly accepts the ADR-001 bucket contract and /healthz is not challenged).

The review correctly identifies the missing purpose check at redemption (shown in the reset-to-verification direction, which follows from the same unbound route at design.md:34), the 20/s-versus-30/s capacity shortfall with correct arithmetic, and the conflict between the 60-minute verification lifetime and ADR-001's 24 hours, while its uncertainties affirm rather than contradict the session and mail hard negatives.

The review completed with grounded, source-cited findings: C1 (body-supplied user_id and delivery_email with a session-free link, critical), M1 (4 × 240 = 960/day < 1,200, high), and C2 (step 4 drops export_tasks holding ~300 deadlined open tasks with no migration, rated high rather than critical); the separate rollback-after-step-4 finding is a grounded additional point about losing all fulfilment paths, and neither hard negative is violated because risk_scores is explicitly called non-gap per ADR-002 and the bearer link is not treated as the defect.

The review correctly found the dropped DELETE events, the non-idempotent balance arithmetic under at-least-once delivery, and the 10.4 h rebuild overrun; it also adds a grounded finding that documents created through the CDC path lack the required open_balance_cents field until their first invoice event, and it violates no hard negative.

The review correctly detects the refund-summation overpayment (C1) and the payout-detail IDOR (C2). Its extra finding is grounded: clearing ledger_entries.payout_id on failure loses the included orders that the detail endpoint promises. The undefined HoldPolicy (M1) appears only as an uncertainty, and the review affirms rather than contradicts the throughput arithmetic (H2) and the $25 carry-forward rule (H1).

All three findings are grounded in the sources and map cleanly to C1, C2 and M1 (the rebuild arithmetic of 37,500 s, 69.12M docs and 3,125 actions/s checks out); the review neither disputes ADR-002's clear-text contact storage nor the steady-state capacity, and its four uncertainties are conditional risks, not counted claims.

The review completed with source-grounded claims and correctly detects C1 (late usage modifies finalized invoices, against ADR-002), C2 (public-read PDFs at enumerable sequential-number URLs) and M1 (2.4M x 150 ms / 12 is about 8.3 h, over R1's 6 h). It adds two grounded findings: the status set cannot tell a carried sub-50-cent invoice from a pending charge on resume, and the existing sub-50-cent path skips the PDF and email that R4 requires. It respects H1 and H2, explicitly calling the prorate_cents claim correct and leaving the carry policy unchallenged.

unsupported_claims.claim: R3 cannot be met whenever a node cannot reach the registry, so the requirement needs scoping or a stale-node mechanism and alerting (severity high).
unsupported_claims.why: ADR-002 (Accepted) states that nodes keep the cached assignment while the registry is unreachable. ADR-002:14-15 explicitly accepts that 'Assignments, including rollbacks, cannot change during a registry outage', and design.md:50-51 cites this policy. Treating the accepted fail-static behavior as a high-severity defect contradicts H4.

unsupported_claims.claim: The 50 s worst case for R3 is unsupported because the 30 s fleet request deadline is undefined and sequential refresh latency is omitted.
unsupported_claims.why: design.md:44-46 states the 30 s fleet deadline as a design fact. The arithmetic (20 s poll + 30 s deadline = 50 s < 60 s, no model load per design.md:41-42) meets R3. Slow sequential fetches with no timeout is speculation with no source evidence. This contradicts H2.

unsupported_claims.claim: The plan names no files to change and lacks tests for SHA-256 mismatch, percent bounds, role checks and pin precedence.
unsupported_claims.why: Nothing in the sources requires the rollout plan to list files or enumerate every test. This infers requirements from a preferred template rather than identifying a defect. Step 2's done criterion (design.md:89) is a stated plan, not a false claim.

verdict.note: No planted defects exist. The review contradicts H4 (it treats ADR-002 fail-static as a high-severity R3 defect) and H2 (it disputes the 50 s rollback arithmetic). It also includes one template-driven finding, while four grounded gaps are valid: canary load-before-route, incomplete stage/transition rules, flag-off back-out with active canaries, and undefined tenant pins.

The review completed, makes concrete source-cited claims, and correctly detects C1 (late usage mutates finalized invoices against ADR-002), C2 (public-read, enumerable PDFs with personal data) and M1 (~8.3 h versus the 6 h R1 target); its three further medium findings are grounded (under-50-cent invoices get no PDF/email per invoice_runner.py:30-37, resume and status gaps plus the carried balance consumed before set_lines, and legacy fallback conflicts with the new unique key), the low-severity 'implementation details open' item is treated as a style observation, and neither hard negative is contradicted (the review confirms prorate_cents behavior and does not criticize the carry-forward policy).

The review completed with concrete, source-cited findings that catch all three planted defects (C1, C2, M1); its two extra findings are grounded and do not contradict H1 or H2: late-usage adjustment charges ignore the 50-cent processor minimum, and the sub-50-cent path in invoice_runner.py:29-32 returns before PDF and email, against R4.

unsupported_claims.claim: The design's 'at most 550 per shard' conflicts with ADR-003's 560/shard admission, so the advertised 2,240 requests/s cannot be admitted and the capacity statement needs reconciliation.
unsupported_claims.why: docs/design.md:9 bounds expected demand (2,200 requests/s including retries, at most 550 per shard); it does not cap admission. ADR-003 (docs/adr-003-refresh-capacity.md:7-11) admits up to 560 per shard, 2,240 total, which is headroom above that demand. docs/design.md:69 correctly cites the 2,240 capacity, so there is no contradiction.

verdict.note: The review completed with one grounded but mistaken finding: it reads the 550-per-shard demand bound as an admission ceiling and disputes the 2,240 usable capacity that H4 affirms, and this case has no planted defects to detect.

The review completed with concrete, source-grounded claims and no planted defects exist to detect; three findings count as valid additional findings: 48-hour cleanup with no timestamp column (design.md:48-50,74), undefined checked_at for manual imports during rollback (design.md:35,60,71-72), and untested R3/R4 paths (design.md:68-70); the fourth finding (unnamed modules, supplier config, auth, enablement, advisory-lock key derivation) is largely a template-driven completeness observation and is not counted, though only its lock-key point is concrete and none of it is factually wrong; the remark that the 390-second budget omits lock and secret-retrieval time appears only under uncertainties and does not assert that R1 is violated, so H4 is not violated, and H1-H3 are respected.

The review detects all four planted defects and adds two grounded findings: the all-tenant rollout with no staged fallback, and the throughput/lag targets given without capacity analysis. Its findings on the flawed parallelism justification and the unfiltered replay are the same monotonic-state defect as C1, so they get no extra credit.

The review completed with three grounded findings that map to C2 (cross-tenant export through the request-body tenant_id), C1 (a hold acknowledged after purge planning is ignored by the queued deletion), and M1 (240 GiB at 2 GiB/min takes 120 minutes, over the 90-minute target); it makes no unsupported claims, violates no hard negatives, and lists 10 separate uncertainties.

unsupported_claims.claim: The rollout leaves required implementation decisions unresolved because it names no migration, job, command, API or UI implementation files and no step implementing snapctl.
unsupported_claims.why: This demands implementation-plan detail from a preferred template rather than identifying a defect in the sources. The design specifies the snapshot_log schema and statuses (docs/design.md:46-48), the response contract (49-50) and snapctl's behaviour (51-52), and states that the job uses the same code as snapctl, which rollout step 2 ships (57-58). The finding itself concedes that no proposed behaviour is shown to be incorrect.

verdict.note: The review completed and is grounded, and it affirms H1-H4 in its uncertainties. Its single finding is a template-style completeness complaint rather than a source-grounded defect, so it is counted as unsupported for this case, which has no planted defects.

The review correctly detects all three planted defects with accurate source citations (the id-only status query, 24 slots / 2s = 720/min < 1,200, and indexing the scalar fetchone()[0] return as result['id']), and its uncertainties are conditional or explicitly consistent with ADR-001/ADR-002, so neither hard negative is violated.

The case has no planted defects, and none of the five rollout and verification findings contradicts H1-H4. Each is grounded in design.md: unlogged cron schemas between steps 1 and 2, no rollback for step 2 plus retention deleting backfilled schemas, no rollout test of R4, step 4's done criterion missing the banner, and R3 unmet before step 4. Finding 1's R4 impact assumes snapctl rejects schemas without a published log row, which the 'published schema' wording supports; finding 2 slightly overstates 'not acknowledged', since design.md:67 says the 14 newest are kept.

unsupported_claims.claim: The plan leaves implementation decisions open: the rollout names no code files, modules, migration file or tests, and the scan-latency dashboard is undefined.
unsupported_claims.why: No source requires a design doc to name code files, migration files or tests. That expectation comes from a preferred template, not from the case. The design refers to the scan-latency dashboard (design.md:93) as an existing artifact, and nothing in the sources shows it is missing or unmeasurable.

verdict.note: The review correctly detects all three planted defects (C1, C2, M1), adds four grounded extra findings (the worker's write to `files` conflicts with ADR-002's IAM restriction, report rows default to the `incoming` bucket, the backlog drain deletes in-flight rows, and the S3 notification payload shape is wrong), violates no hard negative, and makes one template-driven claim that is not supported.

unsupported_claims.claim: The rollout lacks concrete implementation and test steps (named test cases, implementation files, passing verification) for its required behavior changes.
unsupported_claims.why: The sources do not require design docs to name test cases or files to change. docs/design.md:30-38 specifies the status-based resume behavior that replaces src/invoice_runner.py's flow, so the gap the finding describes is the design's proposal, not a defect. The finding infers requirements from a preferred template rather than identifying a contradiction with R1-R5 or the ADRs.

unsupported_claims.claim: The 50 s worst case for R3 is not actually the worst case; a transient fetch failure makes it 70 s, so the stated bound does not justify claiming R3 is met.
unsupported_claims.why: H2: design.md:44-46 correctly bounds rollback at one 20 s poll plus the 30 s request deadline, which is 50 s and under 60 s, with no model load. A ConnectionError in refresh() (rollout.py:38-40) means the registry is unreachable from that node. ADR-002:14-15 explicitly accepts that assignments cannot change while the registry is unreachable, so this case is not a flaw in the R3 arithmetic. The claim that sequential fetch latency uses up the margin has no supporting source evidence.

verdict.note: The case has no planted defects. unsupported_claims.claim: Connection loss after the database commits the pointer switch violates the guarantee that failed imports preserve published quantities, so the design needs indeterminate-commit reconciliation.
unsupported_claims.why: In that scenario the import did not fail: a complete, validated, greater revision was atomically committed (docs/design.md:31-35). R3 (design.md:15) and R2 still hold, since readers see one complete revision. design.md:23 and :36 describe failures that prevent a commit, and PostgreSQL does abort uncommitted work on connection loss. No reconciliation is needed: the next tick fetches the same immutable revision (design.md:47), and the equal-revision path (design.md:33) only updates checked_at. The finding describes an observation ambiguity with no incorrect published state, not a requirement violation.

verdict.note: The review completed and violates no hard negatives, but its single finding is unsupported because an ambiguously acknowledged commit still publishes a correct complete revision and is handled idempotently by the equal-revision path.

unsupported_claims.claim: Nothing in the sources supports four shards carrying 2,200 req/s at no more than 550 per shard; per-shard skew above 1.8% plus retries will cause 503 storms.

unsupported_claims.claim: The design does not define the server outcome for a prior token with the same ID once replay conditions fail, and a client could send a new ID with the old token after 30 s, triggering revocation.
unsupported_claims.why: design.md:44 says superseded tokens return invalid_grant, and :48 says invalid_grant requires login, so the server outcome is defined. design.md:49 forbids starting another refresh, and so a new request_id, until the previous response is durably applied, which rules out the new-ID scenario the finding relies on.

unsupported_claims.claim: Capable clients whose sessions are not enrolled cannot apply any legacy refresh response, so most canary-stage clients would discard successful refreshes and fail after 30 seconds (major).
unsupported_claims.why: Lines 45-49 and 59 describe the rotation flow and its response schema, which carries generation. Nothing applies the 'newer generation' rule (line 46) to legacy responses. Legacy refresh (lines 65-67) issues claims without rotating a refresh token, so applying it cannot replace newer credentials (line 15). The claimed failure comes from the review's reading, not from the sources.

unsupported_claims.claim: The plan relies on ADR-003's per-shard admission limit but has no task to enforce it, so nothing sheds load before a shard exceeds its tested capacity (major).
unsupported_claims.why: ADR-003 is Accepted and its Decision states 'Enforce admission at 560 refresh requests/s per shard' with excess receiving HTTP 503 (ADR-003:9,11). design.md:69 adopts ADR-003 and design.md:61 defines the 503/Retry-After contract. Admission is an explicit accepted decision, not an absent one. Requiring a separate per-file rollout task is a template demand.

unsupported_claims.claim: The completion criterion 'all capable sessions rotate' may never hold because sessions that never refresh never rotate.
unsupported_claims.why: In context, line 75 follows the canary of '1%, 10%, then 100% of capable sessions' (line 70), so 'rotate' means enrolled in rotation, not that each session has performed one. Sessions that never refresh expire at their 30-day deadline (lines 11-12) and stop being live sessions. The finding depends on an over-literal reading.

unsupported_claims.claim: The design leaves the cache writer's correctness-critical behavior and integration undecided (no trigger, version source, files to change or implementation sequence), so the 60-second staleness bound is delegated to the implementer.
unsupported_claims.why: docs/design.md:7 already states the protocol at design level: the worker reads committed PostgreSQL names, writes reject older database versions, and expiry is anchored to the database-read timestamp and never extended past 60 s. That establishes the consistency bound (H4). The finding asks for scheduling details, affected files and an implementation sequence, which are template requirements the rubric says not to infer. src/lookup.py having no write path is not a design defect because the design never claims a writer exists in that file. Treating rollout percentages as missing implementation phases is the same template demand; design.md:13 gives the rollout and rollback gates (H5). The review does not claim the bound or gates are absent, so no hard negative is violated outright, but the defect is not supported by the sources.

verdict.note: The review is complete and grounded, and correctly raises no ADR, retention or fallback false alarms, but its single medium finding demands implementation-template detail beyond the design's already stated write-ordering and expiry rules, so it counts as unsupported rather than a valid additional defect.

The review correctly identifies the refund-model mismatch (C1) and the detail-endpoint IDOR (C2), and adds two grounded findings: the rollback re-send has no age limit, which conflicts with the 21-day and 30-day idempotency limits, and the carried-balance display required by ADR-001 is missing. It raises the undefined HoldPolicy (M1) only as a hedged uncertainty, and it does not contradict H1 or H2.

unsupported_claims.claim: Major: R3's 60 s rollback bound conflicts with the accepted outage exception, so the guarantee overstates supported behavior when nodes cannot fetch a committed rollback.
unsupported_claims.why: The design does not leave the outage case unqualified. docs/design.md:48-51 cites ADR-002 and states that transitions are unavailable and nodes keep the cached assignment during an outage. docs/adr-002-fail-static-serving.md:13-15 explicitly accepts that rollbacks cannot change mid-outage. The R3 arithmetic (design.md:44-46) covers normal propagation. Calling this documented, accepted fail-static trade-off a major defect re-raises the hard negative instead of identifying a real gap.

verdict.note: The review is complete and grounded, and correctly respects H1-H3. Its only finding treats the accepted ADR-002 fail-static rollback exception as a major R3 defect, so it is counted as unsupported and as violating H4; the ten uncertainties are recorded separately and are not false alarms.
